models.name: Model 1 — Component-Level Explicit FE
models.what_it_computes: Femoral component–polyethylene contact pressures, contact areas, sliding distances, cross-shear metrics, and Archard-type wear depth/volume under prescribed kinematics consistent with simulator-style inputs; no surrounding soft tissues.

models.name: Model 2 — Anatomy-Coupled Explicit FE
models.what_it_computes: Joint contact mechanics, backside interface micromotion, ligament constraint reaction forces (via nonlinear springs), cross-shear–dependent wear on the tibial insert under load-driven boundary conditions with malalignment and high-flexion maneuvers.

mechanisms.name: Steady-State Tibial Insert Wear During Level Walking
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Long-term polyethylene volume loss and wear scar evolution drive survivorship and revision risk.

mechanisms.name: Varus–Valgus Edge Loading
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Rim contact elevates peak pressures and local stresses, accelerating wear and risking insert damage.

mechanisms.name: Backside Interface Micromotion and Fretting
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Relative motion at the insert–tray junction contributes to particulate generation and locking feature degradation.

mechanisms.name: High-Flexion Pivoting Cross-Shear
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Combined axial load and transverse pivoting elevates cross-shear, increasing wear rate beyond gait-only conditions.

findings.mechanism: Steady-State Tibial Insert Wear During Level Walking
findings.span: Against six million-cycle datasets with measured gravimetric loss and reconstructed wear scar maps, the RMS difference in wear volume after calibration was 12 percent, and the Jaccard index for the projected wear scar footprint exceeded 0.72, indicating appropriate localization of wear.
These results align with reported sensitivity of pressure and wear to alignment, showing marked local intensification without equivalently large integral wear increases.
We compared simulations with level-walking simulator wear volume and contact patch maps, pin-on-plate cross-shear tests, and tibial insert–tray micro-motion rigs.

Looking forward, the most effective steps to elevate credibility scores into the established tier for the challenging mechanisms are: (1) dedicated edge-loading experiments mapping angulation and lift-off to contact and wear outputs, enabling direct apples-to-apples comparisons with the modeled malalignments; (2) high-flexion pivoting wear tests that report cross-shear metrics alongside volumetric loss to sharpen calibra-tion beyond gait; (3) systematic characterization of insert–tray locking compliance across sizes and tolerances, including post-assembly gap evolution; and (4) expanded uncertainty quantification with validated distributions for friction and lubrication states across activities, thereby tightening predictive intervals.
